## Abstract

ECG-based artificial intelligence (AI) may enable efficient prediction of incident HF risk to facilitate preventive efforts. Prior models are proprietary with modest or inconsistent accuracy. We sought to develop and validate a generalizable and publicly available convolutional neural network to predict incident HF using the 12-lead ECG waveform (Electrocardiogram-to-Heart Failure, “ECG2HF”).

We developed ECG2HF in 94,636 patients receiving longitudinal ambulatory care in Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), and validated in three test sets: MGH, Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH), and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), among 93,868 individuals aged 30–79 without HF. HF events at 10 years were identified using a validated electronic health record-based natural language processing model. Discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). We then compared discrimination and net reclassification (at <10%, 10–20%, ≥20% 10-year risk categories) using ECG2HF versus the 15-component Pooled Cohorts Equations to Prevent Heart Failure (PCP-HF) score.

The test sets comprised MGH (13,954 individuals, 441 events, age 57±13, 48% women), BWH (54,396 individuals, 1,809 events, age 57±13, 55% women), and BIDMC (25,457 individuals, 901 events, age 57±13, 53% women). Over 10 years, the cumulative risk of HF was 4.6% (95% CI 4.1–5.0) in MGH, 5.0% (4.8–5.2) in BWH, and 4.4% (4.1–4.7) in BIDMC. ECG2HF discriminated 10-year incident HF in each test set (AUROC MGH 0.86 [0.84–0.87]; BWH: 0.85 [0.84–0.86]; BIDMC 0.84 [0.83–0.86]). Compared to PCP-HF, ECG2HF provided favorable discrimination (improvement in AUROC MGH/BWH 0.061 [0.025–0.097]; BIDMC 0.038 [−0.0096–0.086]), and net reclassification (NRI MGH/BWH 0.16 [0.077–0.24]; BIDMC 0.23 [0.10–0.35]) of 10-year HF risk.

ECG2HF is a publicly available 12-lead ECG-based AI model that discriminates risk of future HF with favorable and consistent performance across three large healthcare samples from the northeastern US. ECG2HF may enable efficient prioritization of high-risk individuals for HF-related preventive measures.

Heart failure (HF) is a significant public health burden affecting >64 million individuals worldwide.1 The incidence and prevalence of HF are increasing due to population aging and improved survival from related cardiovascular diseases.2 Despite advances in management, HF remains a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality, underscoring a critical unmet need for early risk stratification to enable preventive measures.3

Multiple clinical models have been developed to predict incident HF.4–6 However, most require a number of inputs including demographics, comorbidities, laboratory results, imaging data, and electrocardiogram values.4,5 Even when these data are available, concerns regarding misclassification of clinical variables and the need for cumbersome calculation have limited the uptake of HF risk estimators in real-world clinical care. Furthermore, most models were derived in highly selected research cohorts, which may limit generalizability. The need for better methods to estimate incident HF risk is highlighted by the 2023 Focused Update of the ESC HF guidelines,7 which emphasize the effectiveness of emerging therapies to prevent HF events, but do not endorse any specific risk model for identifying at-risk individuals.

Deep learning approaches have demonstrated the ability to discriminate incident HF risk using the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), a non-invasive, inexpensive, and widely available diagnostic test.8–10 However, existing approaches have been limited by modest accuracy (area under the receiving operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.76),8,9 inconsistent performance (AUROC 0.72–0.81),10 and lack of public availability, limiting access and potential clinical implementation. Furthermore, prior models have been developed using diagnosis codes to ascertain HF events, which are prone to misclassification.11 Contemporary natural language processing (NLP) methods capable of providing clinical endpoint committee-level accuracy for defining HF episodes using free-text data12–14 now provide a unique opportunity to assess whether training on a large number of high-fidelity HF events may result in models capable of discriminating future HF risk with favorable and consistent performance across multiple real-world healthcare populations.

In this study, we develop a publicly available deep learning model to predict incident HF using only the 12-lead ECG, with HF episodes adjudicated using an extensively validated NLP algorithm.12–14 We hypothesized that such a model may facilitate accurate and efficient HF risk stratification across three large ambulatory care samples.

## Methods

### Study samples

Our deep learning-based HF prediction model (Electrocardiogram to Heart Failure, ECG2HF) was developed in previously described samples including patients receiving longitudinal primary and ambulatory cardiology care within the Mass General Brigham multi-institutional healthcare network.15,16 Briefly, patients were aged 18–90 years with ≥2 office visits spaced between 1–3 years apart in a qualifying clinic between 2000–2019, and all patients were linked to a common electronic health record (EHR). For longitudinal analyses, start of follow-up is defined as the second office visit of the earliest qualifying pair, to allow an ascertainment period for baseline clinical characteristics. Based on the implementation of validated risk models, prior work has shown that our cohort selection process and longitudinal analysis structure improve data density, minimize missingness, and reduce selection bias compared to other methods of EHR ascertainment.15

ECG2HF was trained on individuals who had ≥1 ECG performed within three years before the start of follow-up within Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) (Figure 1). ECG2HF was then evaluated among individuals without prevalent HF in an internal test set of MGH patients not included in model training (MGH Test), and two ambulatory care samples from separate hospitals: 1) Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH), and 2) Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC). Given MGH and BWH are affiliated hospitals within a larger healthcare network, we ensured no overlap of individuals or tracings between MGH and BWH.

### Heart failure definition

The study outcome was incident HF, defined using the combination of 1) ≥1 International Classification of Diseases, 9th or 10th revision (ICD 9/10) code for HF, and 2) classification of HF from a transformer-based NLP model trained to detect HF hospitalization using free text discharge summaries. This approach has been extensively validated, demonstrating high classification performance for HF hospitalization (area under the receiving operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.91) against expert clinician review utilizing standardized HF trial criteria in our cohort,12 as well as very good agreement (83–87%) and favorable diagnostic test characteristics (e.g., sensitivity 94%, specificity 84%) compared with gold-standard clinical endpoint committee adjudications in multiple clinical trials.13,14 In each setting, the NLP-based approach provided substantially more accurate classification compared to ICD 9/10 codes alone, which were also assessed in secondary analyses (Supplementary Table 1).12

### ECG acquisition and ECG2HF architecture

ECG2HF is a 1D convolutional neural network designed to predict 10-year incident HF using a single 12-lead ECG (Supplementary Figures 1–2). For training, ECG2HF was exposed to all 12-lead ECGs performed within the three years prior to the start of follow-up in the MGH training set, and weights updated based on performance in the validation subset. As performed previously, since individuals with prevalent HF may provide particularly rich training signal (i.e., they provide clear examples of HF-related changes on the ECG), individuals with prevalent HF were included in ECG2HF training.17 Consequently, for training and validation, time to HF was defined from the date of ECG, where prevalent HF was encoded as a time-to-event of zero. ECGs were inputted as time-series of 5000 voltage measurements for each of 12 leads, sampled at 500 Hz over 10 seconds (tracings sampled at 250 Hz were linearly upsampled to 500 Hz). To maximize model applicability, no specific filtering or pre-processing was applied to the waveform prior to analysis. ECG2HF utilizes an encoding and loss function explicitly accounting for survival time and censoring (Supplementary Methods).18 To ensure model evaluation mirrored the intended clinical use case, only a single ECG was used (the tracing most closely preceding the start of follow-up), patients with pre-existing HF were excluded, and only individuals aged 30–79 years (i.e., the published age range of prior HF clinical scores4) were evaluated. All ECGs were acquired using GE Healthcare (Chicago, IL) machines.

ECG2HF was trained to predict time to first HF event. Given prior evidence supporting improved performance of deep learning models with inclusion of related tasks as secondary prediction targets,17 we trained ECG2HF to simultaneously perform prediction of age, sex, time to death (to explicitly model the competing risk of death), and the presence of an incident HF ICD code in a primary position. This design resulted in improved accuracy for HF compared to other task regimes, and outperformed a model utilizing age and sex as fixed inputs instead of targets (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Figure 3).

### Pooled Cohorts Equations to Prevent Heart Failure (PCP-HF)

We then compared ECG2HF to the validated PCP-HF clinical scores for 10-year risk for incident HF.4 We selected PCP-HF as a comparator given its analogous design as an HF-specific risk stratification tool for ambulatory patients without need for cardiac imaging, similar requirement for 12-lead ECG, and previously favorable performance compared to other prediction scores.4 For this analysis, we utilized a complete case approach. Details of PCP-HF calculation in the test sets are described in the Supplementary Methods.

### Statistical analysis

In each test set, person-time began 30 days following the start of cohort follow-up (see below) and ended at the earliest of an event, death, last encounter or age 90. Death was ascertained using EHR-based definitions and the Social Security Death Index. In each test set, the 30-day blanking period was instituted to reduce misclassification of prevalent cases as potential incident HF events (i.e., events within 30 days of start of cohort follow-up were considered prevalent and therefore excluded from incident analyses, with time zero beginning at the end of the blanking period) (Figure S4).

Our primary metric for discrimination was the time-dependent AUROC at 10 years.19 Since HF events are relatively uncommon, we additionally calculated the time-dependent average precision (AP), which provides a complementary assessment emphasizing the ability to detect high-risk individuals. Analogous to AUROC, AP provides a composite measure of test precision and recall across a range of predictor thresholds. AP values are dependent on the sample-specific event rate, which also serves as the benchmark performance of a completely uninformative model (i.e., a completely uninformative model classifying all individuals as ‘positive’ will achieve an average precision equal to the event rate). Therefore, the ratio of a model’s AP to the event rate provides a metric of relative enrichment for event risk. Using both metrics, we compared ECG2HF to a Cox proportional hazards model including HF as the outcome and age and sex as covariates was used as a reference comparator. Both AUROC and AP were calculated using inverse probability of censoring weights.20

Calibration of absolute risk estimates was assessed by plotting absolute versus predicted risks, fitting corresponding smoothed curves using adaptive hazard regression, and calculating the integrated calibration index (ICI), a measure of the average prediction error weighted by the empirical risk distribution.21 The ICI can be interpreted similarly to alternative error metrics such as the time-dependent Brier score (i.e., an error of zero represents perfect calibration), but the ICI more accurately reflects overall model calibration by explicitly incorporating the observed risk distribution.21 For AP, AUROC, and ICI estimates, 95% confidence intervals were calculated using bootstrapping (500 iterations for AP and AUROC, and 200 iterations for ICI). Models were compared (e.g., ECG2HF versus PCP-HF) by quantifying differences in model metrics, with associated 95% confidence intervals for those differences calculated using bootstrapping (e.g., as implemented in the ‘APtools’ package in R). Here, a 95% confidence interval of the difference exclusive of zero signifies a difference in model performance significant at a two-sided alpha level of 0.05.22

To estimate the effect of ECG2HF implementation, we calculated net reclassification indices (both continuous and categorical at <10%, 10–20%, and >20% 10-year HF risk5). To assess the robustness of our findings, we also performed several sensitivity analyses, including the assessment of a model combining ECG2HF and PCP-HF probabilities and enforcement of a 1-year window between ECG, clinical factors, and start of follow-up (Supplementary Methods).

Analyses were performed using Python v3.10 and R v4.3. Use of Mass General Brigham data and BIDMC data were approved by respective institutional review boards. This study adheres to the TRIPOD-AI and TRUE-AIM reporting guidelines.

### Data availability

The data from Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH), and BIDMC contain protected health information, and individuals did not consent to data sharing. Therefore, these data are not publicly available.

### Code availability

The trained ECG2HF model is publicly available for non-commercial use under an academic software license on the Machine Learning for Health model repository (https://github.com/broadinstitute/ml4h/tree/sf_ecg2hf/model_zoo/ECG2HF).

## Results

### Baseline characteristics

The individuals from MGH were randomly split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets. The training and validation sets together comprise the MGH development set, which includes a total of 94,636 individuals (n=4,949 heart failure events) with 364,304 ECGs (median ECGs per individual: 2 [quartile-1: 1, quartile-3: 4]) Median time between ECG and start of follow-up was 492 days [246, 707]. ECG2HF was then evaluated in MGH Test (13,954 individuals, age 57±13 years, 48% women), BWH Test (54,457 individuals, age 57±13 years, 55% women), and BIDMC (25,457 individuals, age 57±13, 53% women) (Figure 1). Most individuals included from the MGH and BWH samples (and all in the BIDMC sample) were primary care patients. Baseline characteristics were generally similar across the test sets, although BIDMC had a relatively higher proportion of Black patients. Detailed baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1. Characteristics of individuals excluded from the MGH and BWH samples based on the absence of an eligible ECG were generally younger and had a lower burden of comorbidity (Supplementary Table 3).

### Discrimination of incident heart failure

Over 10 years, there were 441 HF events in MGH Test (10-year cumulative risk 4.6% [95% CI 4.1–5.0]), 1,809 HF events in BWH Test (5.0% [4.8–5.2]), and 901 events in BIDMC (4.4% [4.1–4.7]). The cumulative risk of death prior to an HF event was 7.9% [7.5–8.4] in MGH, 8.0% [7.7–8.2] in BWH, and 7.3% [7.0–7.7] in BIDMC.

ECG2HF consistently discriminated 10-year HF in each test set according to AUROC (MGH 0.86 [0.84–0.87]; BWH 0.85 [0.84–0.86]; BIDMC 0.84 [0.83–0.86], p<0.01 versus age and sex for all). AP values demonstrated a consistent ~4-fold average enrichment for HF risk over the event rate (MGH 0.19 [CI 0.17–0.23] with event rate 0.046; BWH: 0.21 [0.20–0.23] with event rate 0.050, BIDMC 0.20 [0.18–0.22] with event rate 0.044, p<0.01 versus age and sex for all) (Figure 2). The cumulative incidence of HF was higher across quintiles of ECG2HF risk in each test set, particularly for the highest quintile (e.g., HF risk in quintile 5: 17.9% [95% CI 16.9–18.9] vs. quintile 1: 0.27% [0.14–0.39] in BWH Test, Figure 3). When compared to the lowest quintile, hazard ratios for HF were markedly higher in the highest quintile (MGH: 57.58 [25.64–129.26], BWH: 76.54 [48.65–120.4], BIDMC 60.55 [34.19–107.2]). Test characteristics of quintile-based thresholds of ECG2HF are shown in Supplementary Table 4. Results were similar when ECG2HF risk was divided into tertiles (Figure S5).

### Calibration of heart failure risk estimates

Median ECG2HF predicted HF risk was similar across MGH Test (10-year estimated HF risk 1.5% [quartile-1: 0.5, quartile-3: 5.2]), BWH Test (1.6% [0.6, 5.5]), and BIDMC (1.6% [0.6, 5.0]) (Figure S6). ECG2HF was generally well-calibrated across the majority of the predicted risk distribution, with ICI values reflecting low estimation error (Table 2). Calibration of the age and sex model was largely similar, although it consistently provided a narrower range of risk estimates around its mean, reflecting more conservative risk estimation (Table 2 and Figure 4).

### Comparison to the PCP-HF scores

After excluding individuals with missing data (MGH/BWH n=54,769, BIDMC n=22,413), we compared the ECG2HF and the PCP-HF scores in 13,642 remaining individuals in the MGH/BWH sample and 3,044 participants in the BIDMC sample. Missing laboratory values (MGH/BWH 85%, BIDMC 91%) were the most common cause of missing PCP-HF score in both datasets.

According to AUROC, discrimination for 10-year incident HF was higher using ECG2HF versus PCP-HF in MGH/BWH (0.80 [0.77–0.83] vs. 0.74 [0.70–0.77], difference 0.061 [0.025–0.097]) and comparable in BIDMC (0.80 [0.76–0.84] vs. 0.76 [0.73–0.80], difference 0.038 [−0.0096–0.086]). Similarly, AP was greater in MGH/BWH (0.26 [0.21–0.31] vs. 0.18 [0.15–0.22] with event rate 0.063, difference 0.079 [0.029–0.14]) and comparable in BIDMC (0.21 [0.16–0.29] vs. 0.17 [0.13–0.22] with event rate 0.064, difference 0.047 [−0.016–0.12]) (Figure 5). The incremental value of ECG2HF over PCP-HF was even higher at shorter prediction intervals, with substantially greater discrimination for 2-year incident HF according to AUROC in both MGH/BWH (0.85 [0.82–0.89] vs. 0.76 [0.72–0.80], difference 0.091 [0.045–0.14]) and BIDMC (0.88 [0.83–0.92] vs. 0.73 [0.66–0.80], difference 0.15 [0.081–0.21]). Two-year AP was also substantially higher in MGH/BWH (0.11 [0.078–0.17] vs. 0.036 [0.027–0.055] with event rate 0.010, difference 0.075 [0.039–0.13]), but comparable in BIDMC (0.10 [0.051–0.19] vs. 0.055 [0.027–0.13] with event rate 0.014, difference 0.047 [−0.035–0.13]) (Figure 5). Predicted risks from ECG2HF and PCP-HF were modestly correlated (MGH/BWH r=0.37 [95%CI 0.35–0.38], BIDMC r=0.36 [0.33–0.39]). A model combining ECG2HF and PCP-HF probabilities achieved moderately higher discrimination than either model alone (MGH/BWH AUROC 0.82 [0.79–0.84], AP 0.27 [0.23–0.32] with event rate 0.063; BIDMC AUROC 0.83 [0.79–0.87], AP 0.24 [0.19–0.32] with event rate 0.064). Distributions of PCP-HF predicted risk stratified by incident HF status are shown in Figure S6.

Both ECG2HF and PCP-HF were generally well-calibrated, with similarly low estimation error in both MGH/BWH and BIDMC (Table 2). At the high end of the predicted risk distributions for both ECG2HF and PCP-HF, there was some tendency to overestimate risk (Figure 5).

ECG2HF provided favorable reclassification over PCP-HF in MGH/BWH (net reclassification improvement [NRI] 0.16 [95%CI 0.077–0.24]), which was driven by both increased sensitivity (case reclassification [NRI+] 13.7% [5.4–20.7]) and increased specificity (non-case reclassification [NRI-] 2.3% [1.3–3.3]). Continuous NRI was also favorable (0.27 [0.16–0.39]). Similar reclassification improvement was observed in BIDMC (NRI 0.23 [0.10–0.35], NRI+ 21.0% [9.1–33.2], NRI- −1.7% [−0.40 to 3.7], continuous NRI 0.23 [0.061–0.39]). Reclassification tables are shown in Supplementary Table 5.

### ECG2HF saliency and behavior

Median waveform analysis demonstrated that individuals at high predicted risk of HF tended to have wider QRS complexes with lower amplitude P waves and longer PR intervals (Figure 6). Saliency maps demonstrated that the ECG P wave, QRS complex, and T wave had the greatest influence on ECG2HF risk predictions (Figure 6). Indeed, the mean (standard deviation) QRS duration was consistently longer among individuals with versus without incident HF (MGH: 100.2ms [27.4] vs. 91.5ms [16.1]; BWH: 107.2ms [30.4] vs. 91.5ms [17.4]; BIDMC: 101.0ms [22.8] vs. 91.4ms [14.4], p<0.01 for all). When analyzed across strata of ECG2HF predicted risk, saliency appeared somewhat more distributed across the waveform for individuals at high predicted risk versus low predicted risk (Figure S7). Saliency maps generated using alternative subsets of patients resulted in very similar patterns (Figures S8–S9).

### Sensitivity analyses

ECG2HF discrimination was similar when HF was defined using an ICD code in a primary position (Supplementary Table 6). Performance of the age and sex model was nearly identical with age modeled as a spline term (e.g., AUROC MGH 0.75 [0.72–0.77]; BWH 0.73 [0.72–0.75]; BIDMC 0.73 [0.72–0.65]). Individuals within higher strata of ECG2HF risk were generally older and had higher rates of HF-related comorbidity (Supplementary Table 7). At the same time, ECG2HF retained substantial discrimination among individuals without common cardiac comorbidities (Figures S10–S11), where an ECG2HF probability in the top quintile remained associated with elevated risk of incident HF (Figure S12). The performance of both ECG2HF and PCP-HF was largely similar when the baseline ascertainment window was restricted to 1 year preceding start of follow-up in MGH/BWH (Supplementary Table 8). We also observed consistent discrimination of incident HF across subgroups of age, with even greater relative value over age and sex amongst the youngest subgroups (e.g., AUROC among age <45 in MGH: 0.83 [95%CI 0.75–0.92] vs. 0.54 [0.41–0.66], difference 0.30 [0.16–0.43]; BWH: 0.90 [0.88–0.93] vs. 0.55 [0.50–0.61], difference 0.35 [0.29–0.40]; BIDMC 0.83 [0.76–0.89] vs. 0.55 [0.46–0.64], difference 0.28 [0.18–0.38]) (Figures S13–S14). ECG2HF discrimination was also generally consistent across ECGs with a clinical diagnostic interpretation of normal versus non-normal (Figures S15–S16), and having a narrow versus wide QRS duration (Figures S17–S18). Discrimination persisted across strata of race (Figures S19–S20), the presence or absence of a pacemaker (Figure S21), and the presence or absence of atrial fibrillation in the clinical diagnostic read of the ECG used for HF risk inference (Figure S22), although AUROC was moderately lower among individuals with a pacemaker and among tracings showing atrial fibrillation. The number of ECGs performed during the ECG ascertainment period (i.e., within 3 years prior to start of follow-up) was generally a weak discriminator of 10-year incident HF (e.g., AUROC (MGH: 0.68 [0.65–0.71], BWH: 0.73 [0.72–0.74], BIDMC 0.69 [0.67–0.71]).

## Discussion

Our study demonstrates that estimation of 10-year incident HF using a single 12-lead ECG is feasible using ECG2HF, a publicly available convolutional neural network. ECG2HF demonstrated consistent predictive utility across three test sets comprising 93,868 ambulatory patients without heart failure. Among individuals with available data, ECG2HF offered favorable performance compared to PCP-HF, a validated 15-component clinical risk tool. Our findings suggest that ECG2HF may offer an opportunity to perform accurate and efficient HF risk stratification in the context of ambulatory care, which is particularly relevant given the growing recognition of the potential of contemporary HF therapies to prevent HF hospitalizations among those at risk, including SGLT2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, and non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.7,23

Our results extend prior observations demonstrating the utility of deep learning models for detection and prediction of HF. Several ECG-based AI models have demonstrated the ability to classify the presence of left ventricular dysfunction.24 More recent efforts focused specifically on the prediction of future heart failure events have demonstrated moderate discrimination (AUROC 0.76)8,9 or inconsistent performance across test samples (AUROC range 0.76–0.81),10 while lack of available model code or weights has limited accessibility and potential clinical application. Furthermore, prior models have been developed using diagnosis codes to ascertain HF events, which are prone to misclassification and may limit model performance.11 ECG2HF extends prior work by leveraging model training in over 90,000 individuals to predict future HF events defined using a validated NLP model capable of adjudicating HF with clinical endpoint committee-level accuracy,12–14 resulting in a freely available ECG-based model delivering robust and consistent 10-year HF prediction across 93,868 individuals spanning three ambulatory healthcare samples.

Our work suggests that the 12-lead ECG contains sufficient information to efficiently stratify risk of future HF. Using only a single 12-lead ECG, ECG2HF estimated 10-year HF risk with substantially greater discrimination than age and sex, with consistent performance across multiple test sets and absolute risk estimates that were generally well-calibrated. Akbilgic et al.8 recently reported an ECG-based neural network trained in approximately 14,000 individuals which achieved an AUROC of 0.76 for incident HF (defined using ICD codes) in an internal test set in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study,8 with similar performance in a subsequent validation in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohort (AUROC 0.76).9 A second model by Dhingra et al. was originally trained to detect left ventricular systolic dysfunction and was found to predict ICD code-defined incident HF in multiple test sets with AUROC range 0.72–0.81.10 Direct comparisons to prior models are not possible as they are not publicly available, and numeric contrasts to published metrics may be misleading to due to differences in study design (e.g., analysis of prospectively acquired ECGs in certain prior studies8–10 versus clinically acquired ECGs in our current analysis). Nevertheless, our results extend previous findings by demonstrating highly consistent discrimination of 10-year incident HF using ECG2HF in three large healthcare samples (AUROC 0.84–0.86, AP 0.19–0.21 representing ~4-fold increase over event rate). We submit that good performance of ECG2HF likely stems from two key design factors: a) close alignment between model training and the downstream use case (i.e., development of a model specifically to predict future HF using an architecture that accounts for survival time and censoring), and b) application of a multiply validated NLP model demonstrating consistently more accurate ascertainment of HF events compared to ICD codes.12–14 Although consistent discrimination is a key strength, we acknowledge that ECG2HF was evaluated solely in ambulatory healthcare-related datasets from a single larger geographic region, and future work is warranted to establish generalizability to other settings (e.g., community cohorts, international populations). In contrast to prior models we have made ECG2HF freely available under an academic use license, facilitating access, future benchmarking, and potential clinical application. Similar to prior models, we acknowledge ECG2HF is a ‘black box’ model with no straightforward translation from ECG input to HF risk estimate; however, using saliency mapping we observed that ECG2HF risk appears to depend most on specific aspects of the ECG waveform such as the terminal portion of the P wave and the early portion of the QRS, suggesting important roles of left atrial depolarization and early ventricular activation on incident HF risk and providing important evidence of clinical plausibility. Future work is warranted to better understand the mechanisms by which ECG2HF can predict incident HF events, and the extent to which such mechanisms may overlap with models focusing solely on left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

Our results suggest that deep learning can identify individuals at high-risk for HF with favorable performance compared to traditional risk factor scores. Compared to PCP-HF, a validated 15-component clinical risk score, ECG2HF offered greater discrimination of HF risk according to multiple metrics, including average precision, which connotes a particular ability to identify the highest risk patients.19 Reclassification analyses also supported the ability to detect high HF risk (up to 20% increase in sensitivity) with comparable or greater specificity. Calibration was generally similar between ECG2HF and PCP-HF, with both scores tending to overestimate HF risk at the higher end of the predicted risk distribution. Of note, most of the potential added value of ECG2HF over PCP-HF was observed in the prediction of shorter-term HF events (e.g., 2 years), which may be more clinically actionable. Greater discrimination of shorter-term events has been shown previously using ECG-based AI models and may highlight a specific role for screening focused on short-term events, and the potential value of updating HF risk estimates over time using serial ECGs. A greater incremental benefit of ECG analysis over clinical variables across shorter time windows may reflect a cumulative effect of clinical factors over time (e.g., age, diabetes), or suggest that ECG data become relatively less informative beyond 2 years. To this end, we found that a model combining ECG2HF and PCP-HF probabilities achieved moderately greater discrimination over either model alone. Future work is warranted to assess whether combination models capable of providing HF risk estimates based on varying data types (including clinical variables when available) may improve risk estimation further by leveraging complementary information. Importantly, the correlation between ECG2HF and PCP-HF was modest, suggesting that ECG2HF is not merely inferring the presence of traditional risk factors. Indeed, ECG2HF continued to discriminate HF risk among individuals with known cardiovascular risk factors as well as ECGs read as non-normal. We speculate that ECG2HF may encode ECG patterns indicative of structural or functional parameters such as cardiac filling pressures25 or degrees of electrical dyssynchrony.26 The ability to refine HF risk even among individuals with known risk factors is consistent with both AHA/ACC27 and ESC7 guidelines on the management of HF which recommend risk stratification among both people at risk for HF and those with established structural heart disease.

We submit ECG2HF may enable efficient prioritization of individuals for HF-focused preventive interventions in an ambulatory care setting. Although risk factor scores like PCP-HF and others are widely available,4–6 model complexity and potential misclassification of inputs have limited clinical implementation and guideline endorsement. Conversely, imaging features (e.g., left atrial size28) and biomarkers (e.g., NTproBNP29) possess predictive value for heart failure, but are less well-suited for routine ambulatory screening given the need for imaging acquisition or blood sample collection. To this end, ECG2HF possesses a substantial advantage by offering risk estimation using an inexpensive diagnostic test routinely performed in the clinic and obtainable within seconds. Furthermore, ECG2HF discriminates HF risk among individuals without common cardiac comorbidities, suggesting opportunities to identify at-risk individuals who may be missed by risk factor scores. Individuals in the highest quintile of ECG2HF consistently had a 10-year risk of incident HF in the range of 15–20%. The ability to identify such individuals may provide the opportunity for intensive modification of risk factors (e.g., blood pressure, weight), or targeted testing (e.g., echocardiography, exercise testing) to identify undiagnosed structural or functional abnormalities. Of note, optimal thresholds for identification of high-risk individuals may differ on the basis of the intended intervention (e.g., starting a medication versus implementing therapeutic lifestyle changes). Future studies are needed to identify optimal methods to integrate ECG-based predictions into existing clinical workflows (including non-academic settings), better understand how patients and providers may respond to ECG-based HF risk estimates,30 and clarify whether risk estimates can be improved by leveraging multiple ECGs over time. We acknowledge that since ECG2HF was evaluated among individuals receiving longitudinal primary and cardiology care, deployment in similar settings would be most sensible. To that end, we envision ECG2HF may be best deployed opportunistically in the setting of routine ambulatory care (i.e., using ECGs obtained for other reasons), although future work is also warranted to assess whether it may also provide a basis for routine ECG acquisition (including potential single-lead ECGs from wearable devices). As imaging and biomarker ascertainment may become increasingly available, there is a future need to quantify the potential incremental value of multi-modal prediction models incorporating ECG-based AI with structural features (e.g., left atrial size28) and laboratory results (e.g., NTpro-BNP29). Overall, given the emergence of medical therapies with potential to prevent incident HF (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors31), there is a need to assess whether targeted administration of preventive therapies, potentially guided by models like ECG2HF, to individuals at the highest risk of HF may improve outcomes. Should risk-based HF prevention become more widespread, it will be important to continually reassess model performance, potentially leveraging predictive evaluation methods designed for scenarios under treatment (i.e., prediction under interventions).32

## Limitations

Our approach has limitations. First, although we rigorously assessed generalizability of ECG2HF by assessment in three ambulatory healthcare datasets including a separate hospital (BWH) and a separate healthcare system (BIDMC), we acknowledge that participants represented individuals receiving ambulatory healthcare within a single broader geographic location (New England region of the United States). Future work is warranted to establish the predictive utility of ECG2HF in other settings (e.g., population-based samples), and validate performance for real-time or prospective use. Second, our analyses utilized 12-lead ECGs performed for clinical indications, selecting for individuals who tended to be older and with greater comorbidity. Although the longitudinal ambulatory samples we analyzed were constructed using an approach shown to reduce bias compared to selection solely based on available data,15 selection on the basis of an ECG introduces bias since ECGs are not a standard screening test in routine primary care,33 and may lead to overestimation of absolute HF risk. Although the requirement for an ECG itself cannot be the driver of observed HF risk prediction performance (as all individuals included had an ECG performed), it may affect model generalizability and future work is therefore warranted to assess performance using prospectively acquired ECGs. We note, however, that performance of the PCP-HF clinical score generally in line with prior reports4 (both discrimination and calibration) supports the representativeness of our samples. Third, although we submit use of a validated NLP model to accurately ascertain heart failure is a key strength (AUROC 0.93), we acknowledge there remains potential for misclassification of HF events, and there is likely some tradeoff with lower sensitivity versus ICD codes alone. Nevertheless, model performance remained robust when using ICD codes to define HF events. If perfect HF classification were available, we suspect that the consequent reduction in false positives could lead to improved performance by removing inappropriate training signals and preventing the erroneous penalization of low predictions among individuals who did not actually have HF. Fourth, use of EHR data sources limits sensitivity to detect HF events that may have occurred outside of the linked EHR. However, prior results demonstrate that our sample design enriches for individuals engaged in longitudinal ambulatory care, maximizing data density and completeness.15 Fifth, given our goal of estimating HF risk using only relatively inexpensive and routinely ascertained diagnostic tests (e.g., 12-lead ECG), we did not compare ECG2HF to models utilizing imaging features (e.g., left atrial size28) or blood-based biomarkers (e.g., NTproBNP29). As an example, we note limited availability of baseline echocardiograms (~30%) and NTproBNP measurements (<10%) in our MGH and BWH samples. Sixth, use of a convolutional neural network architecture facilitates analysis of subtle aspects of the ECG waveform, but limits the ability to identify specific features that may contribute to HF risk predictions. Seventh, we compared ECG2HF to the PCP-HF clinical score among the subset of individuals with available clinical data, mirroring the real-world scenario in which risk scores are calculable only among individuals with sufficient data. In contrast, we derived and validated ECG2HF in larger samples without requirement for PCP-HF score components, facilitating greater statistical precision and highlighting the potential value of estimating HF risk without the need for detailed clinical variables.

## Conclusion

ECG2HF is a publicly available deep learning model to predict 10-year risk of incident HF using only a single 12-lead ECG. ECG2HF discriminates future HF risk consistently across three large northeastern US healthcare samples, offers favorable predictive utility compared to the PCP-HF clinical risk score, and outperforms published metrics for prior deep learning-based models predicting incident HF. ECG2HF may facilitate automated and efficient HF risk stratification at scale, to prioritize susceptible individuals for potential preventive interventions.

## Abstract

Aortic pulsatility index (API) and cardiac power output (CPO) are strongly associated with mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock, but their association with outcomes across broader cardiopulmonary disease is unknown.

The objective of the study was to examine the association of API and CPO with clinical outcomes across a hospital-based cardiovascular cohort.

We used a hospital-based longitudinal, observational cohort of patients who underwent right heart catheterization. We calculated API = aortic pulse pressure/pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and CPO = (cardiac output x mean arterial pressure)/451. We used multivariable Cox models to examine the association of API and CPO quartiles with all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and heart failure hospitalization (HFH).

A total of 4,278 patients (age 64 ± 11 years, 36.5% women, 35.3% prior heart failure) were included. Over a mean of 7 ± 3.2 years, there were 1,552 deaths, 1,429 MACE, and 991 HFH. Patients in the lowest API quartile had double the risk of death (HR: 2.06; 95% CI: 1.71-2.47), nearly double the risk of MACE (HR: 1.94; 95% CI: 1.65-2.30), and close to triple the risk of HFH (HR: 2.82; 95% CI: 2.31-3.45) compared to the highest quartile (all P < 0.001). Similarly, those in the lowest vs highest CPO quartile had greater risk of death (HR: 1.25; 95% CI: 1.08-1.46), MACE (HR: 1.51; 95% CI: 1.29-1.78), and HFH (HR: 1.90; 95% CI: 1.57-2.30; all P < 0.005).

Although lower API and CPO are known prognostic metrics in patients with cardiogenic shock, these findings support their broader utility across the spectrum of cardiovascular disease.

Key words: heart failure, hemodynamics, prognosis, right heart catheterization

## Abstract

Patients with advanced heart failure (HF) have a limited prognosis with a median survival of 6 to 12 months.1, 2, 3 Accurately assessing risk is critical for guiding clinical decision-making, particularly when determining the need for advanced therapies.4,5 Traditionally, prognostication in HF has relied on clinical characteristics and measures such as cardiac output (CO) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). Although these standard metrics provide useful information, they often fail to fully capture the complexity of HF, particularly in patients with severe or advanced disease.4,6, 7, 8

Recent studies among individuals with advanced HF and cardiogenic shock have examined integrated hemodynamic indices, including the aortic pulsatility index (API) and cardiac power output (CPO), and demonstrated their additive prognostic value when compared with clinical and traditional hemodynamic measures.4,5,9, 10, 11 These indices are derived from invasive hemodynamic measurements obtained during right heart catheterization (RHC) and each capture a distinct dimension of cardiac physiology. Given their unique construction and established prognostic potential, there is growing interest in examining their application beyond patients with end-stage heart disease.5 For example, although CPO has been primarily used in the context of patients with cardiogenic shock, emerging studies have begun to explore its role in patients with chronic HF and in the ambulatory setting.12,13

Although these metrics have been primarily studied in the context of patients with advanced HF and cardiogenic shock, with some studies extending to HF without shock and ambulatory settings, their application and prognostic significance across a broader sample of individuals with cardiopulmonary disease remains unclear.14, 15, 16 We sought to examine these integrated metrics in the context of a hospital-based cohort of individuals undergoing clinically-indicated RHC to ascertain the association of both API and CPO with clinical outcomes across the spectrum of cardiovascular disease. Specifically, we delineate clinical and echocardiographic correlates of API and CPO, and examine associations with all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and HF hospitalization. We hypothesized that lower API and CPO would be associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality, MACE, and HF hospitalizations across a broad cardiovascular cohort.

## Methods

We used a hospital-based longitudinal, observational cohort of patients who underwent clinically-indicated RHC between January 2005 and December 2016 at Massachusetts General Hospital.17 In patients who underwent multiple RHC, only the initial RHC was used for the purpose of this study. The cohort was constructed to encompass a broad patient base, with exclusion of critically ill patients. After excluding individuals with acute myocardial infarction (MI) occurring on the same day as RHC, cardiac arrest or shock within 24 hours of RHC, mechanical ventilation, intra-aortic balloon pump, history of heart or lung transplant, adult congenital heart disease, history of valve replacement, or those on dialysis, there were 8,285 individuals in the sample. We further excluded individuals missing key hemodynamic parameters (n = 3,924) or follow-up (n = 83), leaving a final sample of 4,278. This study was approved by the Mass General Brigham and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center Institutional Review Boards.

Demographics and clinical characteristics were obtained from the medical record at the time of RHC and included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), hypertension, diabetes mellitus, prior history of MI, prior history of HF, prior lung disease, and hyperlipidemia. Echocardiographic data obtained closest to and within 1 year of RHC were collected (available for n = 2,888 individuals).

Hemodynamic parameters recorded during RHC included systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP), mean right atrial pressure, pulmonary artery systolic and diastolic pressure, and mean PCWP. CO and cardiac index were preferentially assessed using thermodilution, and assumed Fick CO and cardiac index were utilized if thermodilution was not available (n = 261, 6% of total sample). API was calculated as aortic pulse pressure/PCWP, and CPO was calculated as: (CO × mean arterial pressure)/451.4

Participants were followed longitudinally after RHC, and the primary outcome for this study was all-cause mortality, whereas secondary outcomes included occurrence of MACE and HF hospitalization (HFH). All outcomes from this study were ascertained from the medical record. MACE was defined by the occurrence of HF admission, acute MI, cerebrovascular accident, or transient ischemic attack. Designation of prior HF was defined based upon review of individual clinical history upon presentation for RHC. The follow-up period for each individual was defined as time from RHC to time of event, or latest encounter recorded in medical record, whichever came first.

### Statistical analysis

Baseline characteristics are summarized by API and CPO quartile using the mean ± SD, median with 25th and 75th percentiles (Q1, Q3) or count (percentage). Differences across API and CPO quartiles were assessed using the chi-squared test, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), or Kruskal-Wallis test as appropriate. The distributions of API and CPO were capped to limit the influence of extreme outliers, with maximum values of API and CPO set to 5 standard deviations above their respective means (<0.01% of high values set to upper limit: API 27.7, CPO 2.74). Both API and CPO were natural log-transformed (LN) due to skewed distributions, and effect sizes expressed per 1-SD increase.

Cross-sectional clinical and echocardiographic correlates of API and CPO were examined using age- and sex-adjusted linear regression models. We then examined the association of both API and CPO with incident clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, MACE, and HFH. We first examined Kaplan-Meier curves of API and CPO quartiles with each of the clinical outcomes and used log-rank tests to examine the differences between quartiles. We then used multivariable cause-specific Cox models to account for competing risk of death for nonfatal outcomes, adjusted first for age, sex, and additionally for BMI, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, prior MI, prior HF, and prior lung disease with results presented as the HR with 95% confidence intervals (CI). We checked the proportional hazards assumption using Schoenfeld residuals, and included a time-varying covariate for API analyses due to minor proportional hazards violations. In exploratory analyses, we analyzed the primary models by presence or absence of prior HF, inpatient vs outpatient status, and left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥50% vs <50%. Finally, we investigated the relative performance of API, CPO, and both API and CPO together relative to a baseline model using Uno’s C-statistics in predicting our clinical outcomes of interest across the entire follow-up period. We accounted for multiple comparisons in primary analyses by applying a Bonferroni correction for 6 tests (2 predictors x 3 outcomes) resulting in a P value <0.008 (0.05/6) as statistically significant and a P value <0.05 deemed suggestive. All analyses were conducted using STATA (version 19.5; StataCorp, 2025) and SAS software, Version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., 2023).

## Results

We studied 4,278 individuals with a mean age of 64 ± 11 years, 36.5% women, 85.5% White race. Across the entire sample, 71.9% of individuals had hypertension, 28.5% had diabetes mellitus, 22.4% had prior MI, 35.3% had prior HF, and 17.0% had prior lung disease. The median (Q1, Q3) API was 4.29 (2.74, 6.56), whereas the median (Q1, Q3) CPO was 0.94 W (0.74, 1.17).

### Association of API and CPO with clinical comorbidities and echocardiographic measures

### Model performance metrics of API and CPO

We examined C-statistics to quantify model discrimination of adverse cardiovascular outcomes with the addition of API, CPO, and their combination to a base model of clinical covariates (Table 4). C-statistics of the clinical model for predicting all-cause mortality, MACE, and HFH were 0.690 (95% CI: 0.673-0.707), 0.628 (95% CI: 0.610-0.647), and 0.659 (95% CI: 0.645-0.673), respectively. ## Discussion

Both API and CPO reflect cardiac performance and are associated with adverse outcomes in individuals with cardiogenic shock.4, 5, 6,11 Our study examines these integrated hemodynamic measures across a broader spectrum of patients with cardiovascular disease who underwent clinically indicated RHC. Our findings are as follows: 1) history of HF, lower LVEF, and the absence of hypertension were consistently associated with worse API and CPO; however, other clinical correlates were distinct between these 2 metrics, with older age, female sex, and lower BMI associated with worse CPO, and younger age, male sex, and higher BMI associated with worse API; 2) both lower API and CPO were independently associated with a greater risk of mortality, MACE, and HFH, with similar results among individuals with and without known HF; and 3) API and CPO improved discrimination of future risk of adverse cardiovascular events when compared with clinical variables alone, with most of the improvement in discrimination attributed to API. Taken together, our findings suggest that the utility of these integrated hemodynamic metrics may extend beyond patients with cardiogenic shock and more broadly inform prognosis in patients across the spectrum of cardiovascular disease.

Of the 2 integrated metrics, CPO has been more widely used given its strong association with inpatient mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock, subsequently resulting in its incorporation into many cardiogenic shock algorithms.18, 19, 20 CPO is proportional to stroke work of the heart and thus reflects total energy output and mechanical work of the heart.4,5,21 Changes in CPO are mediated by changes in the mean arterial pressure and CO, and thus CPO also incorporates both aspects of pressure and flow. CPO’s prognostic ability in cardiogenic shock thus far has been most impactful in shock states due to acute insults (ie in the setting of acute MI) rather than chronic insults (ie chronic HF), with the thought that patients with chronic heart disease can largely maintain their stroke work with cardiac remodeling over time and thus have “normal” CPO despite an extensively diseased cardiac substrate.4,5,21,22 Some studies suggest that noninvasively measured CPO has prognostic value in chronic HF with reduced ejection fraction; however, data in patients with preserved ejection fraction are limited, and its use has not been widely adopted in either setting.12,13,23 Our findings expand upon the previous literature, demonstrating in a large cohort across a broad spectrum of cardiopulmonary disease that low CPO is strongly associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes regardless of baseline HF status. Interestingly, although CPO predicts MACE and HFH among those with prior HF, we did not find an increased risk of mortality, in line with current literature of CPO’s limited prognostic ability in chronic HF states.4,5,24 Furthermore, association with adverse outcomes was attenuated among the subgroup of individuals with LVEF ≥50%.

Although CPO reflects a patient’s given mechanical work, fluctuations in API are mediated by changes in systemic BP and left-sided filling pressures; thus, API reflects a patient’s given loading conditions, inherent cardiac efficiency, and ventriculoarterial coupling.4,5,25 API can be thought of as the left-sided correlate of the pulmonary artery pulsatility index, which has previously been shown to be associated with right ventricular failure and adverse outcomes in patients with shock, advanced HF, and broader samples with cardiovascular disease.4,9,26, 27, 28, 29 Similar to CPO, we find that low API is associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality, MACE, and HFH. The unique construction of the API equation, however, enables it to capture clinical features that CPO is unable to capture alone. API’s direct integration of real time hemodynamic and loading conditions enables the detection of pathophysiologic decline that may be obscured in CPO by compensatory remodeling that preserves stroke work.5,6,25 In a subanalysis of the ESCAPE trial, API was associated with freedom from death, heart transplant or LV assist device placement at 6 months in patients with acute decompensated HF without cardiogenic shock, whereas CPO was not.22,30 In a validated clinical simulation model, both low API and CPO were able to predict adverse clinical outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock in the setting of acute MI; however, only API was associated with adverse outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock in the setting of chronic HF.25 Another study assessing prognostic ability of hemodynamic indices to predict freedom from advanced therapies (ie heart transplant, inotropic support, mechanical circulatory support) or death in patients with advanced HF, both API and CPO were associated with the primary endpoint at 30 days; however API had a greater area under the curve.6 Our study extends upon these findings, demonstrating that in a broad cardiovascular cohort, lower API was associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality regardless of prior HF status or baseline ejection fraction, whereas CPO was not. Furthermore, we found that the addition of API to clinical variables was associated with greater improvement in discrimination metrics for adverse outcomes when compared with the addition of CPO.

When evaluating C-statistics to assess the additive prognostic value of API and CPO beyond our baseline clinical covariate model, we found that although each metric individually improved the predictive performance for adverse cardiovascular outcomes, the greatest discriminative ability was achieved when both were used in combination. We also found that API, rather than CPO, was the primary driver of this improved discriminatory function in the combined model. A prior study has similarly shown that although CPO, API, and pulmonary artery pulsatility index are each predictive of adverse clinical outcomes, concordant utilization of both CPO and API was associated with the greatest freedom from advanced therapies (including heart transplant and LV assist device placement) or death at 6 months in patients with advanced HF.14 Our findings extend this work by demonstrating the complementary prognostic value of API and CPO in a diverse cardiovascular cohort over a substantially longer follow-up period. Further studies are needed to examine the clinical applicability of these integrated hemodynamic indices in guiding risk stratification, clinical decision-making, and timing of advanced therapies across broader samples. Furthermore, repeat hemodynamic evaluation may provide additional clinical insights and help recalibrate risk over time.

Interestingly, when examining clinical correlates of both CPO and API, we found that prior HF and lower LVEF were associated with worse CPO and API. By contrast, other clinical correlates were disparate, including older age, female sex, and lower BMI which were associated with worse CPO, and younger age, male sex, and higher BMI which were associated with worse API. To date, relationships between API and CPO with demographic factors such as age, sex, or BMI have not been well described. Higher BMI has been associated with increased CO in obesity, particularly during exercise and in high-output HF, which may partly explain our findings of higher BMI in patients with lower API, but does not explain its discordance with CPO.25,31 Similar to CPO, lower API was also strongly associated with adverse echocardiographic parameters, underscoring the importance of an intact cardiac anatomical substrate for hemodynamic efficiency.5 However, API is limited by its reliance on aortic pulse pressure and may be confounded by altered aortic compliance, such as with stiffness or calcification, potentially explaining the lack of association between diabetes mellitus (a known metabolic cardiovascular risk factor) and lower API in our cohort. Interestingly, previous MI was associated with lower CPO but not API in our cohort, which may be partially explained by evidence that post–MI patients with residual LV dysfunction can exhibit reduced stroke work despite preserved systemic BP and normal ventricular filling pressures.32

For both API and CPO, interpretation of values remains challenging due to the lack of standardized reference ranges. Prior studies in cardiogenic shock have identified a CPO threshold of < 0.53 W as conferring the greatest in-hospital mortality risk for patients with cardiogenic shock.4,11,18,33 The median value of 0.62 W in our lowest CPO quartile is slightly higher but broadly consistent with these data and extends their relevance to a larger, more heterogeneous cardiopulmonary population. With regards to API, a cutoff of 1.45 has been linked with the need for advanced therapies in patients with advanced HF.6 The median of our lowest API quartile of 1.94 suggests a more conservative cutoff may be more appropriate for prognostication across a broader cardiovascular cohort. In this context, further studies are needed to delineate clinical utility of patient- or disease-specific cut points for both API and CPO.

### Study limitations

This study has several important limitations. Given the observational nature of the cohort design, inferences cannot be made regarding the causality between measured exposures and outcomes, and residual confounding may be present, including limited contemporary therapies and individual factors such as access, adherence, and socioeconomic status. Another limitation of our study was lack of data on indication for RHC and the reliance on billing codes to ascertain clinical outcomes, which may be subject to potential misclassification. Although our cohort included a large diverse spectrum of cardiovascular disease, those more likely to have cardiogenic shock where these hemodynamic metrics have previously been studied, including those with same day MI or cardiac arrest, or those requiring mechanical circulatory support, were excluded. Furthermore, our sample included patients who underwent clinically indicated RHC and is subject to selection bias, limiting generalizability of our study findings to other samples.

In sum, although API and CPO have been primarily used in risk stratification in patients with cardiogenic shock, we demonstrate that both hemodynamic metrics have prognostic potential across a diverse spectrum of cardiovascular disease. Specifically, patients in the lowest API and CPO quartiles are at a greatest risk for all-cause mortality, MACE, and HFHs. Taken together, our findings extend existing studies and suggest that both metrics can potentially be used to risk-stratify patients across a broader cardiovascular disease population.

COMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE: In a longitudinal observational cohort of patients with a broad spectrum of cardiopulmonary disease, API and CPO were associated with increased risk of all-cause mortality, MACE, and HFH. These results suggest that API and CPO may more broadly inform prognosis beyond patients with cardiogenic shock.

TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Future studies should investigate whether API or CPO can guide risk-stratification to inform clinical decision making including referral for advanced therapies.

# Sex Differences in Right Ventricular, Pulmonary Vascular, and Integrated Hemodynamic Measures of Cardiac Function in HFpEF and HFrEF

**Authors:** Meihan Guo; Juhi K Parekh; Emily S Lau; Leah B Kosyakovsky; Louisa A Mounsey; Eugene Pomerantsev; Michael H Picard; Jennifer E Ho

**Affiliations:** 1 CardioVascular Institute and Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 2 Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 3 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Sex differences in clinical presentations of heart failure (HF) are pervasive, yet differences in invasive hemodynamic measures across HF subtypes remain incompletely characterized. Understanding these distinctions is critical, as sex‐specific physiology influences disease progression and prognostic assessment in HF.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 1818 patients with HF who underwent clinically indicated right heart catheterization, stratified by preserved versus reduced ejection fraction. We examined the association of sex with invasive hemodynamic measures of right ventricular, pulmonary vascular, and left ventricular function using multivariable linear regression.

We studied n=709 individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) (44% women, mean age 68±10 years) and n=1109 with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) (26% women, mean age 64±12 years). Women and men had similar measures of right ventricular function across HF subtypes (multivariable‐adjusted P>0.05 for all). However, women with both HFpEF and HFrEF exhibited worse pulmonary vascular function, with significantly higher pulmonary vascular resistance and lower pulmonary artery compliance (multivariable‐adjusted P<0.001). Women with both HFpEF and HFrEF had similar cardiac power index, but higher aortic pulsatility index (P=0.01 for HFpEF; P<0.001 for HFrEF).

Among a large hospital‐based sample of patients with HF, women and men exhibited similar indices of right ventricular function, despite women having worse pulmonary vascular function. Cardiac power index was similar between sexes in both HFpEF and HFrEF, whereas aortic pulsatility index was higher in women with HFrEF. Taken together, sex differences in hemodynamic measures were largely similar across individuals with HFpEF and HFrEF. Future studies are needed to delineate clinical implications of these sex differences.

## What Is New?

- In a large hospital‐based cohort of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, women and men exhibited similar right ventricular function, despite women demonstrating worse pulmonary vascular function and higher aortic pulsatility index.

## What Are the Clinical Implications?

- Recognition of these sex differences in hemodynamic abnormalities may help better understand well‐described clinical differences among women and men with heart failure.

Sex differences in cardiovascular physiology are well‐described and may underlie distinct predisposition, clinical presentation, and hemodynamic manifestations of heart failure (HF) among women versus men. For instance, in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), women have worse diastolic reserve compared with men, as evidenced by greater elevations in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) indexed to workload and higher mitral E/e′ ratio both at rest and during exercise. 1 , 2 In addition, women with HFpEF typically have lower cardiac output (CO) and lower stroke volume reserve compared with men. 1

Whether these sex differences extend to other invasive hemodynamic measures that reflect right ventricular (RV) function and pulmonary vascular (PV) function in the context of HF remains unclear. Further, little is known about sex differences that may be shared versus distinct among individuals with HF with preserved versus reduced ejection fraction. Lastly, emerging integrated metrics—such as cardiac power index (CPI) and aortic pulsatility index (API)—have been recently used to assess cardiac performance in the setting of cardiogenic shock and advanced HF. 3 , 4 Higher CPI reflects better cardiac performance and portends improved survival, even after adjustment for conventional metrics such as PCWP and ejection fraction. 3 Lower API is independently associated with progression to advanced therapies or death, with superior predictive value compared with CO. 4 However, the prognostic utility and sex differences in these integrated indices among less critically ill HF patients remain unclear.

In this study, we sought to comprehensively characterize invasive hemodynamic measures in a broad hospital‐based sample of individuals with HFpEF versus HFrEF. We specifically investigated sex differences across hemodynamic measures of RV, PV, and left ventricular (LV) function, incorporating both traditional and novel integrated measures. Given the central role of hemodynamic measures in therapeutic decision‐making and prognosis, elucidating sex‐based differences in invasive hemodynamic measures stratified by HF subtype has the potential to refine risk stratification and shed further light into well‐described sex differences across clinical presentation and outcomes in HF.

## METHODS

Statistical code and analytic methods will be made available from the corresponding author upon request. The data are not available to other researchers for purposes of reproducing the results. Informed consent was not required/waived.

### Study Sample

We studied consecutive ambulatory and hospitalized patients who underwent clinically indicated right heart cathterization (RHC) at Massachusetts General Hospital between 2005 and 2016. Among individuals with multiple procedures, only the initial RHC was included. Of the 10 306 cases identified, we excluded individuals with acute myocardial infarction (MI) on the day of catheterization, cardiac arrest or shock within 24 hours, mechanical ventilation, intra‐aortic balloon pump, history of heart or lung transplant, complicated adult congenital heart disease, prior valvular replacement, or dialysis dependence (n=887). We also excluded cases with missing key clinical covariates (n=484), missing patient identifiers (n=398), or missing hemodynamic data (n=252), resulting in 8285 individuals. Of these 8285 individuals, 2062 had clinical HF, and had echocardiography within 1 year of RHC to classify HF into HFpEF (LVEF≥50%) versus HFrEF (LVEF<50%). From this group, we further excluded individuals with missing critical hemodynamic variables—yielding a final study sample of 1818 participants. A secondary sample of 1162 participants was derived after further excluding those with missing data on variables CPO and API. This study was approved by the appropriate Institutional Review Boards.

### Clinical and Echocardiographic Assessment

Clinical characteristics were obtained from medical records at the time of RHC and included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, and the presence of comorbidities such as chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), history of MI and valvular disease. OSA was identified using, Ninth and Tenth Revision (ICD‐9 and ICD‐10) codes from the electronic medical record. Multimorbidity was defined as the presence of 2 or more chronic health conditions, and included obesity, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, prior lung disease, OSA, and history of MI. 5 Echocardiographic data within one year of RHC were reviewed to extract both quantitative and qualitative assessments of LV size and function. When multiple echocardiograms were available within one year of RHC, the study performed closest to the catheterization date was used. LV hypertrophy was defined using sex‐specific thresholds for LV mass index, with values >95 g/m2 for women and >115 g/m2 for men, in accordance with established clinical criteria. 6 , 7

### Invasive Hemodynamic Assessment Via RHC

Key hemodynamic parameters recorded at the time of RHC included resting blood pressure, heart rate (HR), mean right atrial (RA) pressure, pulmonary artery (PA) systolic and diastolic pressure, and mean PCWP. CO and cardiac index (CI) measurements were primarily obtained using the thermodilution method; when unavailable, the assumed Fick cardiac output and index were used. Both were indexed using the Mosteller formula for body surface area (BSA). 8 SV was calculated as CO divided by HR, and SV index (SVI) was indexed to BSA. Non‐physiologic values were set to missing (<1% of measurements).

We examined the following hemodynamic indices of RV function: RA/PCWP ratio, a surrogate of RA pressure relative to left‐sided filling pressure, RVSWI (RVSWI=0.0136×SVI×[mean PA–RA pressure]), an estimate of RV contractile work; and PA pulsatility index (PAPi=[PA systolic–PA diastolic pressure]/RA) integrated preload and afterload to characterize RV‐pulmonary artery coupling. For PAPi, RA was imputed as 1 if listed as 0. We additionally examined pulmonary effective arterial elastance/RA pressure (Ea/RA pressure=[mean PA pressure–PCWP]/[SV×RA pressure]) as a reflection of PV load and right‐sided congestion. 9 , 10 We evaluated the following PV indices: PVR (PVR=([mean PA pressure–PCWP]/CO)×80), transpulmonary gradient (TPG=mean PA pressure–PCWP), and PA compliance (PAC=SV/[PA systolic–PA diastolic pressure]). Lastly, integrated measures of cardiac function were calculated among a subset of n=1162 (64%) of individuals who had available matched blood pressure data, which included cardiac power output (CPO=CO×mean arterial pressure [MAP]/451), CPI (CPI=[MAP×CI]/451) and API (API=[systolic–diastolic pressure]/PCWP). 3 , 11

### Statistical Analysis

Baseline clinical, echocardiographic, and hemodynamic characteristics were summarized by HF subtype and stratified by sex. Distributions of hemodynamic variables were examined, natural log‐transformed if skewed, and standardized to a mean of 0 and SD of 1. To minimize the influence of outliers, the distributions of RA/PCWP ratio and PAPi were winsorized. For RA/PCWP, values were limited to a range of 0.1 to 3.5; for PAPi, values were bounded at a minimum of 0.3 and a maximum of 30 as in prior studies. 12

We pre‐specified 6 primary hemodynamic measures including RA/PCWP ratio, PAPi, PVR, PAC, CPI, and API. In separate analyses for HFpEF and HFrEF, we examined cross‐sectional associations of sex with hemodynamic variables using multivariable linear regression models. The model first accounted for age, and additionally for other comorbidities including BMI, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, chronic lung disease, OSA, and prevalent MI. For indexed values including RVSWI, CI, SVI, and CPI, analyses were adjusted for age and comorbidities but not BMI or BSA. Exploratory analyses adjusted non‐indexed measures for BSA in place of BMI. To account for multiple comparisons, we applied a Bonferroni correction, setting the statistical significance threshold at P value <0.008, with suggestive P<0.05. All analyses were performed using STATA software, Version 18.5 (College Station, Texas).

Among individuals with HFpEF, women and men had similar age (68±10 versus 68±10 years), BMI (31.2±8.6 versus 30.2±6.1 kg/m2), prevalence of hypertension (78% versus 80%) and prior valvular disease (60% versus 57%, P>0.05 for all). Differences in comorbidities were observed, with certain conditions being more prevalent among men compared with women, such as chronic kidney disease (5% versus 10%), diabetes (35% versus 43%), hypercholesterolemia (80% versus 86%), OSA (15% versus 24%), and prior MI (19% versus 28%). By contrast, chronic lung disease was more prevalent among women (33% versus 24%; P<0.05 for all).

Among individuals with HFrEF, women and men had similar age (64±12 versus 64±12 years), BMI (28.2±7.6 versus 28.9±6.3 kg/m2), and prevalence of chronic kidney disease (5% versus 5%) and diabetes (35% versus 36%, P>0.05 for all). Men had higher prevalence of hypertension (75% versus 64%), hypercholesterolemia (83% versus 76%), OSA (14% versus 7%), previous MI (49% versus 33%), but lower prior valvular disease (37% versus 47%, P<0.05 for all).

Among individuals with HFpEF, men had greater multimorbidity compared with women (defined as 2 or more comorbid conditions, 75% versus 67%). Similarly, among individuals with HFrEF, men had greater multimorbidity than women (71% versus 64%; P<0.05 for both).

### Sex Differences in Echocardiographic Measures of Cardiac Structure and Function

Across both HF subtypes, we found that women had smaller LV dimensions and LV mass index compared with men. In addition, women had higher LVEF compared with men. Specifically, among those with HFpEF, the median LVEF was 66% [IQR 59%–73%] versus 64% [IQR 57%–70%], in women versus men, respectively; Similarly, among women with HFrEF, the median LVEF was 30% [IQR 23%–40%] versus 26% [IQR 20%–35%] in men. The prevalence of LV hypertrophy among women with HFpEF was higher than men (50% in women versus 41% in men, P=0.015). In contrast, among individuals with HFrEF, 74% of women and 65% of men met LV hypertrophy criteria (P=0.003).

Regarding RV function, there was a borderline difference in the prevalence of RV dilation (19% versus 14%, P=0.06) between men and women with HFpEF, although this did not reach statistical significance. RV systolic dysfunction (10% versus 7%, P=0.10) was similar between sexes. By contrast, more men than women had RV dilation and dysfunction among individuals with HFrEF (33% versus 16%, P<0.001 for RV dilation, 47% versus 31%, P<0.001 for RV dysfunction).
